stem: A48-year-old man who had a liver transplant three years earlier is admitted to the Emergency Department with nausea and vomiting. which has steadily worsened over the past 48 hours. He has recently been taking a course of clarithromycin for a respiratory tract infection. He is taking a tacrolimus-based regimen for immunosuppression post-transplant. His blood pressure is 122/72 mmHg, with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 92 g/L 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 4.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 123×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 223 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: Clarithromycin is a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor, and tacrolimus is primarily metabolised by CYP3A4.When clarithromycin is used in conjunction with tacrolimus, it can lead to a significant accumulation of the immunosuppressant. This accounts for the nausea and vomiting seen here. Accumulation of tacrolimus also leads to QT prolongation, which can lead to the development of torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia. Patients with torsades de pointes require regular monitoring of their tacrolimus levels. Liver Enzyme Inhibition Media explanations.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic complaining of aching pains affecting her shoulders and hips, which are particularly bad in the morning when she is extremely stiff for an hour or more. She has hypertension and takes a beclomethasone inhaler for asthma but is otherwise well. She is seen in the afternoon at the clinic and only mild stiffness affecting her hips and shoulders is confirmed. Investigations: What is the most appropriate initial intervention? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/l 115-160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 281×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 88 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Erythrocyte sedimentation 62 mm/hr 10 mm/hr rate(ESR)
explanation: This patient has hip and shoulder pain, with morning stifness lasting45minutes and is in the right age bracket for a diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica. The elevated ESR also fits with the diagnosis. Prednisolone 15mg daily for three weeks,followed by gradual tapering, is an appropriate initial intervention. Symptoms should resolve quickly. In the event that they are not controlled, there is potential to increase the dose to 25mg daily. Symptoms consistent with temporal arteritis should prompt an increase in corticosteroids to 60 mg/day. Polymyalgia Rheumatica Media explanations.

stem: A75-year-old man comes to the Outpatient Department for review. He has recurrent episodes of incontinence, problems starting and stopping passing urine and has had to get up 2-3 times per night for many years. His General Practitioner (GP) has noted a gradual increase in his creatinine levels over the past 6-9 months. His blood pressure is 123/84 mmHg and his pulse is 67 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft and he is mildly tender in the suprapubic region. A rectal examination reveals a smooth, enlarged prostate Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 137 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 242×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 192μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Prostate-specific antigen(PSA) 7.0 mg/l 5mg/l Urine Protein and blood negative Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient most likely has overflow incontinence related to benign prostatic hypertrophy. Two options exist: Finasteride 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, such as finasteride, reduce androgen production and hence impact on prostate.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He has suffered two syncopal episodes over the past year. He has a family history of heart disease; his father died in his bed at the age of 29. His elder brother is also thought to have died of a cardiac arrest six months earlier, again after being found dead in bed. On examination,the patient's blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg and his pulse is 72 bpm and regular. His chest is clear and he has no heart murmurs. What is the most likely underlying cause of these cardiovascular events?
explanation: Brugada syndrome differs from a number of other causes of ventricular arrhythmia in that episodes of ventricular fibrillation are very often seen at night while patients are asleep. This pattern is in marked contrast to conditions such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and long QT syndrome where rhythm disturbance is often related to exercise. If there is clinical suspicion of the condition, patients are given an infusion of ajmaline to unmask the electrocardiogram(ECG) changes and make a formal diagnosis. Q. Answered Flagged External Links It is inherited in an autosomal-dominant fashion and a significant proportion of cases are caused by sodium channel gene mutations. Brugada syndrome is usually resistant to intervention with antiarrhythmic agents. Therefore, an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is the most appropriate intervention to reduce the risk of sudden death in these patients. stem: A 69-year-old man who has metastatic prostate cancer with bone pain comes to the clinic for review. He tells you that despite taking regular paracetamol, naproxen and 45 mg of slow-release morphine twice a day, he still has substantial pain affecting both humeri, both femurs and his lumbar spine. He is awaiting radiotherapy. nvestigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 93 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 122×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 135μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L What is the most appropriate way to manage the patient's pain?
options: 7.5 mg oral morphine 2- to 4-hourly as needed (PRN)
15 mg oral morphine 2- to 4-hourly PRN and slow-release morphine
explanation: This is the correct dosing of morphine for breakthrough pain where the total daily dose of oral morphine is divided by 6.With a total dose of 90 mg, this makes 15mg used every 2-to 4-hourly. In the event this patient's Cr level worsens, the dose of morphine may need to be reduced because of accumulation in renal failure, or a switch made to an agent that does not accumulate in renal impairment such as fentanyl. Pain relief- palliative care explanations.

stem: A 38-year-old man is reviewed in the Cardiology Clinic following an anterior myocardial infarction. He is a non-smoker who was well until he presented to the Emergency Department with a myocardial infarction. His blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg and his pulse is 68 bpm and regular. There are no signs of cardiac failure. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 140 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 240×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 105μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Total cholesterol 8.8 mmol/L 5.2 mmol/L Triglycerides 3.7 mmol/L 0.45-1.81 mmol/L Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) 4.1 mmol/L 4.1 mmol/L High-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) 1.0 mmol/L ≥1.6 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's dyslipidaemia?
explanation: This patient has premature cardiovascular disease and mixed dyslipidaemia with significant elevation of both.

stem: A 56-year-old woman who has rheumatoid arthritis presents to the Renal Clinic for review. Her General Practitioner has noted a steady rise in her creatinine level over the past year, with proteinuria. She takes regular naproxen for pain relief. Blood pressure is 152/90 mmHg and pulse 78 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m2. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 92 g/l 115-160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.3×10/L 7.3 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 281×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 186 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Protein 2+, blood negative How has non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug(NSAID) use contributed to the patient's renal impairment?
explanation: Drug Nephrotoxicity explanations Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug act as COX inhibitors. Prostaglandin E2 and 12 are crucial to maintaining adequate renal perfusion via arteriolar dilatation in times where compromise could occur such as in patients with hypovolaemia or cardiac failure. COX inhibition causes reduced levels of prostaglandin E2 and 12.Over the longer term, this leads to chronic renal damage with elevated Cr and hypertension with proteinuria.

stem: A 59-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He has had two episodes of pain and swelling affecting his right first metatarsal joint in the past five months. These episodes responded to ibuprofen. Examination in the clinic reveals no evidence of tophi and his metatarsal joint between attacks appears normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 138 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 261×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 122μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Serum urate 0.55 mmol/L 0.15-0.41 mmol/L What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient's episodes of pain over the first metatarsal joint are likely to have been episodes of gout and there is clear elevation of uric acid levels above the upper limit of normal. ALlopurinol is the initial treatment for gout and should, therefore, be initiated at a dose of 100 mg daily, but it can be uptitrated to a maximum dose of 900 mg to control uric acid levels. Lower doses should be used in renal failure. Gout Media explanations.

stem: A 45-year-old woman, who is known to have acute intermittent porphyria(AIP), is admitted to the Emergency Department with a lower respiratory tract infection. She has been started on antibiotics by her General Practitioner a few days earlier. She is anxious and agitated. Her blood pressure is 152/90 mmHg, and her pulse is 95 bpm and regular. There are crackles at the right base on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/l 115-160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 12.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 241×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 131 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's hyponatraemia?
explanation: Erythromycin is the least safe of the antibiotics listed. It is a potent inhibitor of CYP3A4 and can precipitate an exacerbation of AIP. It potentially explains this patient presenting with hypertension and hyponatraemia with a respiratory tract infection only a shorttime following prescription of antibiotics. Azithromycin is a much less potent inhibitor of CYP3A4 and can potentially be used in porphyria. Acute Intermittent Porphyria Media explanations.

stem: A71-year-old smoker presents to the Renal Clinic for review. He has hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease(COPD) and has been found by his General Practitioner to have dipstick-positive haematuria on three occasions over the past six months. His blood pressure is 135/82 mmHg and pulse 80 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no masses. His body mass index(BMI) is 25 kg/m2. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin(Hb) 135 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 291×10/L 150-400×109/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 131μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Protein negative, blood 2+ What is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: Haematuria in a smoker without other symptoms should prompt consideration of an underlying bladder tumour. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE) guidelines recommend cystoscopy as the most appropriate investigation where a tumour can be visually identified and biopsied to confirm the diagnosis. In the event cystoscopy is normal, then contrast CT could be considered to rule out transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter or renal carcinoma. Transurethral resection is usually possible for small bladder tumours. Kidney and Urinary Tract tumours explanations.

stem: A72-year-old man comes to the Ophthalmology Clinic, complaining of deteriorating vision, particularly at night. He has problems with a dark patch appearing in the visual field of the left eye, which takes a few minutes to clear, as well as flashing lights and he feels there is glare around headlights when he drives the car at night. Ophthalmoscopy reveals bilateral drusen,more marked on the left than on the right. What is the most likely cause of the patient's visual symptoms?
explanation: This patient's symptoms, particularly with respect to poor night vision, glare and difficulties with dark adaptation, coupled with the presence of optic nerve drusen, fit with a diagnosis of age-related macular degeneration. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy, fluorescein angiography and ocular coherence tomography are all part of the typical workup. Wet age-related macular degeneration can be managed with vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitors, which reduce angiogenesis and blood vessel leakage and slow the progression of visual loss. Q.

stem: A 48-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department as an emergency medical patient with ascending weakness which began a few days earlier and has now left her unable to mobalise. She suffered a diarrhoeal illness some two weeks earlier which has now resolved. Her blood pressure is 122/72 mmHg and her pulse is 82 bpm and regular. There is marked limb weakness below the knee, with some weakness of the hip flexors. Reflexes are diminished bilaterally. A lumbar puncture reveals elevated protein. Which complication related to the patient's underlying condition is the most concerning?
explanation: This patient has ascending lower limb weakness some two weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. This raises the possibility of Guillain-Barré syndrome(GBS), which is supported by the lumbar puncture findings. A significant risk from GBS is respiratory muscle weakness, which increases the risk of respiratory failure and opportunistic infection. For this reason, serial measurements of forced vital capacity are crucial in the management of GBS. Plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin are both potential ways to manage the condition. Q.

stem: A 75-year-old woman presents to the clinic for review. She has failed to tolerate two different bisphosphonates due gastrointestinal upset and does not want to attend the hospital for periodic infusions. She is a smoker of ten cigarettes per day. Her body mass index(BMI) is 20 kg/m. She has a previous left Colles fracture. Her T-score is -3.5. What is the most appropriate next intervention for the patient's osteoporosis?
explanation: Denosumab is the most appropriate option here, given the patient has a T-score of-3.5, is a smoker, with a low body mass index(BMI) and has not tolerated bisphosphonates. It has a significant advantage in that it can be administered once every six months via subcutaneous injection, ensuring compliance. Denosumab is a RANK-ligand inhibitor which reduces osteoclast activity and pre-osteoclast to osteoclast maturation, which leads to downregulation of bone resorption, similarly to bisphosphonates. Q.

stem: A58-year-old man is reviewed after returning to the Coronary Care Unit following stenting of his left main stem for an acute anterior myocardial infarction (MI). His blood pressure has dropped to 85/50 mmHg and his heart rate has slowed down to 38 bpm. The monitor shows ST-segment elevation with a ventricular escape rhythm. He looks pale and sweaty. He fails to respond to 3 mg of atropine. What is the most important next intervention?
explanation: Transcutaneous pacing is the intervention of choice here for a patient who has complete heart block and hypotension as a result of an anterior myocardial infarction. Any prolonged period of hypotension could significantly exacerbate myocardial ischaemia and prompt intervention is crucial. Planning should be made to proceed to temporary transvenous pacing as early as possible. Given the heart block has occurred as a result of an anterior myocardial infarction, the risk of permanent heart block is significantly increased. Coronary heart block is far more common in inferior myocardial infarction and if it does occur following an anterior myocardial infarction, the risk of mortality is also increased. Dificulty: Easy Q.

stem: A34-year-old woman who has asthma presents to the clinic for review. Her current medications include beclomethasone 200 mg twice daily(BD), montelukast 10 mg daily and a salbutamol inhaler as needed (PRN). She admits to coughing every night and has filled her whole quota of salbutamol early. She has bilateral quiet wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Her peak flow is 420 litres/minute in the clinic(550 predicted). What is the most appropriate next treatment step?
options: Add omalizumab 300 mg every four weeks
explanation: This patient has asthma which is not yet under control and adding salmeterol, a long-acting beta-agonist, is the most appropriate next step for this patient. There is evidence that using three therapeutic modalities is preferred to increasing the dose of inhaled corticosteroids at this stage and the approach is endorsed by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE) clinical pathways. In the event that control is not improved after the addition of salmeterol, increasing the dose of inhaled corticosteroid is the most appropriate next step. Q.

stem: A 22-year-old woman complains of urethral discharge and pain on intercourse. She has recently had unprotected sexual intercourse with a new partner. Speculum examination reveals cervical discharge which shows Gram-negative diplococci on microscopy. What is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: Gonorrhoea is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a Gram-negative diplococcus. It results, as here,in urethral discharge. It may cause dysuria, pain and bleeding on intercourse, but it is asymptomatic in up to 50% of women who become infected. The British Association for Sexual Health and HIV(BASHH) guidelines suggest that a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone is the intervention of choice. Ciprofloxacin and azithromycin are potential alternatives. Q.

stem: A74-year-old man who has moderate aortic stenosis is listed for colonoscopy because of anaemia and positive faecal occult blood testing. His cardiovascular symptoms are stable and valve replacement is not currently planned. What is the most appropriate pretreatment before the patient's colonoscopy?
options: Metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for three days
explanation: Antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended for patients with valve lesions undergoing dental procedures, upper or lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract endoscopy,genitourinary tract investigations or upper or lower respiratory tract investigations. In the event patients are considered at significant risk of endocarditis and the benefit-risk of prophylaxis is considered positive, then amoxicillin is a typical prophylactic intervention, given as a single dose of 3 g. Q.

stem: A 27-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department, having awakened from sleep while on a long- haul flight with severe posterior neck pain. He is 1.94 m in height and had his neck extended in his seat. He is anxious; his pulse is 90 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg. He has partial ptosis and miosis affecting his left eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient is very tall and has neck pain after hyperextending his neck. The symptoms of partial ptosis and miosis are consistent with Horner syndrome. It occurs due to compression, stretching or hypoperfusion of sympathetic nerve fibres within the carotid wall. Investigations include duplex carotid angiography and usually magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) with angiography because the detection rate of lesions is superior for MRI vs computed tomography. Anticoagulation may be considered in an attempt to prevent embolic phenomena leading to a large stroke. Q.

stem: An 18-year-old man comes to the Neurology Clinic for review, having suffered a generalised tonic-clonic seizure while at college. He admits to involuntary limb jerking, particularly in the early morning, which has become worse over the past few years. He is awake and conscious during the episodes of limb jerking. He reports that his brother and father suffer from a similar condition. Neurological examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is an autosomal-dominant form of epilepsy, which is characterised by involuntary myoclonic jerks which gradually progress over a number of years; eventually, generalised tonic-clonic seizures develop. The intelligence quotient (IQ) is usually preserved. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are typical interventions. Q.

stem: You are examining data from a recent biomarker study and have been told by the statisticians that the data is positively skewed. Which of the following will be found in the data?
options: Median will be less than the mean
Median will be more than the mean
Mean will be less than the mode
Median will be less than the mode
Median will be the same as the mode
explanation: In a positively skewed distribution there is a positive tail to the distribution, this means that the mean is greater than both the median and the mode.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department after suffering a motor vehicle accident and splenic rupture. She suffers an anaphylactic reaction to blood transfusion. This is the first time she has received a blood product and she is usually well. Which deficiency is the most likely cause of the patient's anaphylaxis?
explanation: lgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency. Most patients with IgA deficiency are asymptomatic, although some develop recurrent bacterial infections and are at an increased risk of autoimmune diseases such as coeliac disease. Prevalence is between 1 in 100 and 1 in 1000 individuals, depending on ethnicity.

stem: A 26-year-old rugby player comes to the Emergency Department with acute right calf pain. He is unable to plantar flex his right foot. Which of the following muscles is most likely to have been injured?
explanation: The gastrocnemius, one of the calf muscles, along with the soleus and plantaris, is key to plantar flexion of the foot. Tears of the muscle are a common sports injury and can usually be managed conservatively with rest, ice, elevation and anti-inflammatory medication.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with bipolar disorder presents to the Renal Clinic for review. She is passing5 litres of urine per day, even after stopping lithium, and has been given a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. Her blood pressure is 125/80 mmHg,with a postural drop of 15 mmHg on standing. She tells you she is thirsty all the time. What is the most appropriate next step in the patient's treatment?
explanation: Thiazide diuretics and a low-salt diet can considerably reduce urine output in diabetes insipidus. Mild volume depletion associated with a weight reduction of 1-1.5 kg can result in≥50% reduction of urine output. Further reduction in urine output is achieved in proportion to a reduction in salt intake managed by the patient. Where these measures are ineffective, a non-steroidal drug can be added. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 69-year-old man with advanced emphysema presents to the Emergency Department, complaining of sudden-onset shortness of breath and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. His blood pressure is 110/75 mmHg, pulse 100 bpm and regular and oxygen saturation 88% on air. Breath sounds are decreased on the left-hand side. Chest X-ray reveals a 2.5-cm rim of air, consistent with a left pneumothorax. What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Air aspiration and admit for oxygen therapy
Air aspiration and progress to chest drain if not resolved
Pain relief and discharge for review in 24 hours
Size 8-14 Fr chest drain and admit
explanation: This patient has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease(COPD) and presents with a large symptomatic pneumothorax. The best option is insertion of a formal chest drain, with informed written consent. Conservative management with either air aspiration or observation is not appropriate, given the risks of further enlargement of the pneumothorax and decompensation. Once the chest drain is in situ,admission for observation is indicated. Dificulty:Average.

He is also short of breath and has developed intermittent fevers over the past few weeks. His rheumatoid arthritis is treated with infliximab and methotrexate. His temperature is 37.7°℃ and his blood pressure is 135/82 mmHg. There is an erythematous rash on sun-exposed areas of his face and arms.You note an effusion affecting his left knee and flexion is limited. Which of the following antibodies is most associated with the patient's presentation?
