stem: A 38-year-old woman is diagnosed with osteomalacia after presenting with proximal myopathy and borderline low calcium. She is prescribed vitamin D tablets. Which of the following is a recognised action of vitamin D?
options: Decreased calcium absorption from the gut
Decreased phosphate absorption from the gut
explanation: Vitamin D has important effects on immuno-inflammation, including maintaining the balance between T- helper 1 and T-helper 2 activity. Decreasing the T-helper 1 response mitigates inflammation and tissue damage. Vitamin D upregulates the T-helper 2 response which is anti-inflammatory. Difficulty.

stem: You are investigating targeting ribonucleic acid(RNA) splicing as a target for intervention in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Where does RNA splicing occur?
explanation: Ribonucleic acid(RNA) splicing involves the processing of pre-messenger RNA(mRNA) into mature mRNA. During splicing, introns are removed and the remaining exons which code for a given peptide are joined together. Splicing takes place within the nucleus during or immediately after transcription. Without splicing, the pre-mRNA cannot be successfully translated into a peptide. Splicing errors are thought to result in a number of neurological diseases, including familial Parkinson's disease linked to chromosome 17 and frontal-temporal dementia. Difficuty.

stem: You are recruiting patients into a smoking cessation study and want to compare baseline smoking rates between ethnic groups. Which of the following statistical tests is the best way to do this?
explanation: The Tukey's range test is the most appropriate tool for statistical analysis here. It is ideal in this case because it can be used to determine if means across different populations are statistically different from each other. It identifies whether the difference between the means is greater than that expected by the standard error, making it ideal in this case to determine if any observed differences in smoking rates are observed purely by chance. Difficulty.

stem: A 70-year-old man who is a retired demolitions contractor presents to the clinic because of a steadily worsening dry cough and shortness of breath over the last nine months. He has failed to respond to a high- dose fluticasone and salmeterol inhaler prescribed by his General Practitioner. He smokes ten cigarettes per day. His blood pressure is 139/85 mmHg and his pulse is 80 bpm and regular. There are fine inspiratory crackles to the mid zones bilaterally on auscultation of the chest. There is pitting oedema of both ankles. Pulmonary function testing reveals a restrictive lung picture. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's respiratory symptoms?
explanation: Dificulty.

stem: A32-year-old woman who is treated with sertraline for depression is brought to the Emergency Department by an ambulance. She is drowsy, agitated and confused. According to her partner, she has been taking St John's wort,in addition to her sertraline, in an attempt to wean herself off the antidepressant. On admission, her temperature is 39.2℃, blood pressure 155/95 mmHg and pulse 98 bpm. Her pupils are dilated;she is sweating excessively and has a tremor. There is inducible clonus and hyperreflexia. Intravenous fluids are commenced. Which of the following interventions would be most useful in easing her symptoms?
explanation: Cyproheptadine is a H1 receptor antagonist with non-specific 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A antagonist properties. This patient has serotonin syndrome, almost certainly as a result of taking St John's wort, in addition to her usual sertraline therapy. Features of serotonin syndrome include confusion, agitation and disturbed consciousness. Examination reveals pyrexia, hypertension, tachycardia, tremor,hyperreflexia and clonus. By blocking the activity of serotonin, cyproheptadine may significantly improve symptoms, although evidence of benefit mostly comes from small case series. Dificulty.

stem: A19-year-old high jumper presents to her General Practitioner complaining of pain over her forefoot. She says it came on all of a sudden and it has been too painful to train for some weeks. There is pain and swelling over the forefoot. What is the most likely cause of this patient's pain?
options: Avascular necrosis of the second metatarsal head
Fracture of the proximal second phalanx
explanation: Avascular necrosis of the second metatarsal is known as Freiberg's disease and is seen most commonly in young women. It may be related to stress or trauma, the most likely cause of this patient's presentation. The disease is thought to occur because the blood supply to the second metatarsal head is slightly tenuous and may be interrupted because of local injury. A sclerotic and flattened metatarsal head is seen on X-ray. Difficulty.

stem: A57-year-old man is started on ramipril 5mg daily for treatment of hypertension. His General Practitioner is concerned that his creatinine level has risen from 108 to 120 μmol/l over the last week. His potassium level has remained stable at 4.9 mmol/L. His blood pressure has fallen from 152/95mmHg to 139/80 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reduce the dose of ramipril to 2.5 mg
Reduce the dose of ramipril to 1.25 mg
explanation: This patient has shown an acceptable reduction in blood pressure and the rise in creatinine level associated with therapyinitiation is modest at around 10%.Only where it approaches 20% or more are concerns raised, involving measuring creatinine and potassium levels two weeks later. A30-50% increase should prompt assessment of volume status and possible temporary discontinuation of the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)inhibitor. Dificulty.

stem: A55-year-old man with a previous gambling problem is reviewed in the Parkinson's Disease Clinic following a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease. He is very concerned as he has read that certain medications used to treat his condition may increase the risk of restarting his gambling behaviour. Which of the following medications is the most suitable option for this patient?
explanation: Procyclidine is a centrally acting anticholinergic agent. It is usually prescribed three times a day in early Parkinson's disease and may be useful in managing tremors. As it does not act through the dopaminergic pathway, it is an option for this patient who is particularly worried about compulsive gambling. He may well, however, require additional medication which acts via the dopamine receptor within a relatively short period. Difficulty.

stem: A75-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with symptoms of severe anaemia. Her haemoglobin has been checked by the General Practitioner (GP) and found to be 60 g/L. She is wearing a bracelet to say she should only receive irradiated blood. What is the main reason for using irradiated blood for this patient?
explanation: Prevention of graft-versus-host disease is the primary reason for using irradiated blood products. A number of situations exist where irradiated blood products are recommended. Examples of these include.

stem: A37-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department, complaining of severe anal itching. She tells you that she has young children who had similar symptoms recently and were diagnosed with threadworm infection. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Threadworms are common and highly contagious. Infection is particularly seen in families with young children. Scrupulous hygiene can eliminate infection over a period of weeks, although in practice, medication makes managing the condition much easier. Mebendazole is the default intervention for adults and children aged above two years. Albendazole is a potential alternative option.

stem: A53-year-old man is referred to the clinic for hypertension control. His current medications are ramipril 10 mg and amlodipine 5 mg, yet his blood pressure measured at the General Practice Surgery is persistently above 149/95 mmHg. His heart rate is 72 bpm and regular and his heart sounds are normal. His body mass index is 23 kg/m. There are no masses on abdominal palpation. Investigations: Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 135 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.6×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 240×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
explanation: Hypertension Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It has the advantage of lowering blood pressure without affecting blood glucose control. For this reason, it is considered a second-or third-line agent in the treatment of hypertension and is the most appropriate intervention here.

stem: A 45-year-old woman of Afro-Caribbean descent with type ll diabetes is referred to the clinic for advice. Her General Practitioner is concerned because her finger-prick blood glucose levels are consistently in the range of 14-18mmol/L, although her glycated haemoglobin(HbA1c) is relatively well-controlled at 51mmol/L. Apart from diabetes, she is relatively well. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 98 g/l 115-160 g/L White cell count(WCC) 6.5×10/L 4.0-11.0×10/L Platelets (PLT) 238×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 91μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L HbA1c 51 mmol/mol 48 mmol/mol What is the most likely cause of the disparity in glucose measurements?
explanation: Sickle Cell Anaemia Media explanations Sickle cell trait occurs in approximately 300 million people worldwide. Generally, people with sickle cell trait have no symptoms, although some patients may suffer significant haemolysis and display other features, including recurrent haematuria and renal impairment. Although this patient has no symptoms of sickle cell trait, chronic haemolysis reduces the average red blood cell lifespan, limiting the time over which it can be glycosylated. This leads to a reduction in HbA1c vs actual measured blood glucose.

stem: A75-year-old woman is reviewed on the Critical Care Ward after her neurological status deteriorated the morning after admission, with a sodium level of 112 mmol/L. She has gone from being confused and combative to being unable to move. Her most recent sodium level is measured at 132 mmol/l and she has been treated with 1.8% sodium chloride infusions. What is the cause of the patient's neurological deterioration?
options: Shift of water out of neurones
explanation: Monitoring of the rate of sodium correction is crucial to prevent central pontine myelinolysis, the likely diagnosis here. In the event that sodium is corrected too quickly, then intracellular charged proteins, which maintain cellular integrity during hyponatraemia, do not have time to alter their charge polarity. This leads to a rapid efflux of water out of neurones, leading to loss of myelin and features of central pontine myelinolysis. Sodium should only be rapidly corrected where serum sodium can be closely monitored and correction should be slow.

stem: An 18-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He is concerned about cancer risk, as his sister and mother died of breast cancer. He has melanocytic pigmentation around his mouth, affecting the buccal mucosa, the sole of his feet and the palm of his hands. A colonoscopy has revealed multiple hamartomatous polyps. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. It is associated with perioral and mucosal melanocytic pigmentation, as seen here, and with hamartomatous polyps. Gastrointestinal cancers associated with Peutz-Jeghers include colorectal, gastric, small bowel and pancreatic cancers. Women with Peutz-Jeghers have a markedly increased lifetime risk of breast(32-54%), ovarian (21%) and cervical(10%) cancers. This accounts for this patient's family history of breast cancer.

stem: A 45-year-old man is reviewed by his General Practitioner because of substantial weight gain of 10 kg over the past year. He has also developed type Il diabetes and has poorly controlled blood pressure despite two oral agents. His blood pressure is 155/93 mmHg and his pulse is 84 bpm and regular. His body mass index is 37 kg/mand he has abdominal striae. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 137 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 6.6×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets (PLT) 309×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate (HCO-) 34 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 118 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glycated Hb(HbA1c) 57 mmol/mol 48 mmol/mol What is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: This patient's weight gain, together with hypertension, diabetes and metabolic alkalosis, is suspicious for hypercortisolism/Cushing syndrome. Out of the options given, a 24-hour urinary cortisol assay is the best initial screening test for Cushing syndrome. Ideally, three collections should be made as cortisol excretion can fluctuate. Confirmatory screening, alongside urinary cortisol, for Cushing includes midnight salivary cortisol assay and low-dose dexamethasone suppression testing. Adrenocorticotrophic hormone(ACTH) should also be tested. In the event it is elevated, pituitary magnetic resonance imaging is the next step. If it is suppressed, adrenal imaging should be considered.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department for the third time over the past six months, complaining of intermittent abdominal pain and bloating. She had two normal colonoscopies and one normal upper gastrointestinal(GI) endoscopy. You understand her grandfather died of bowel cancer three years earlier at the age of 78.Routine examination is entirely normal. She is unable to work because of worrying about the pain. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/l 115-160 g/L White cell count (WCC) 6.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 241×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.8 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 81μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Somatoform disorders explanations This patient's excessive worry about abdominal pain and bloating, despite a number of normal examinations, is consistent with a diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder. The trigger may well have been the death of her grandfather from bowel cancer.

stem: A74-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic for review, she has been taking high dose vitamin
options: Increased phosphate absorption from the gut
Increased phosphate excretion via the kidneys
explanation: Vitamin D increases the absorption of both calcium and phosphate from the gut. It is a class Il steroid hormone receptor agonist, promoting enterocyte differentiation. It also suppresses the release of the parathyroid hormone(PTH), regulates osteoblast function and facilitates PTH-induced osteoclast activation and bone resorption. It is also involved in maintaining muscle strength. Proximal myopathy is often seen as an initial presenting symptom of osteomalacia.

stem: A 38-year-old woman who works on a salad stand at a music festival is admitted with sudden onset left- sided weakness. She tells you she has been ill for a few days with a high temperature and diarrhoea. Her temperature is 37.9℃, blood pressure 137/84 mmHg and pulse 84 bpm and regular. She has bruising and petechial haemorrhages affecting both upper and lower limbs. There is left-sided upper motor neurone facial weakness. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 89 g/L 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 12.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 54×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 192μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Protein 1+, blood+ Which of the following is the most useful blood test in establishing the diagnosis?
explanation: Microangiopathic Haemolytic Anaemia explanations This patient's presentation is consistent with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura(TTP), complicated by a cerebral event, potentially related to Escherichia coli0157 infection and production of Shiga toxin. Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia is seen and thromboses are related to a deficiency in ADAMTS13 activity where large von Willebrand factor multimers on the endothelial surface are no longer cleaved. Levels of10% are strongly indicative of an underlying diagnosis of TTP. In this case, with a likely cerebrovascular event, plasma exchange is the most appropriate next step.

stem: A 61-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension is admitted to the Emergency Department with central crushing chest pain of 40 minutes'duration and ST-segment elevation in leads II IIl and aVF on the electrocardiogram(ECG). Which coronary artery is most likely to have been occluded?
explanation: Occlusion of the right coronary artery is responsible for around 80% of inferior myocardial infarctions, which is the territory affected here. Given the changes are confined to the inferior leads, it is most likely the distal portion of the artery which is occluded here.

stem: A 23-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by the Police. They found him trying to break into the house across the road, however he appeared agitated and delusional at the scene. He tells you that he removed the light bulbs in all rooms of his flat and covered the windows with black paper to prevent the government from broadcasting messages into his brain. He also says that he broke into his neighbour's flat as she has red curtains which is a sign that she is a Russian spy. He refuses examination and has obvious signs of self-neglect. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged This patient has evidence of primary delusional perception (the interpretation of the change of curtain) and thought insertion (the government broadcasting into his brain). He has no insight as to his symptoms. This fits with a diagnosis of acute schizophrenia, as does the self-neglect. Atypical antipsychotics, such as risperidone, are theinitial intervention of choice in patients with acute schizophrenia. Benzodiazepines may be of value in the short term for controlling anxiety and aggression.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the onboard doctor on a cruise ship after becoming acutely unwell with profuse vomiting and watery diarrhoea which began all of a sudden. They docked on the Tunisian coast some 18 hours earlier.Ten other passengers are unwell. His temperature is 37.9°℃, blood pressure is 95/70 mmHg, pulse is 100 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft and generally tender, with very active bowel sounds. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Norovirus is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's acute gastrointestinal symptoms and the outbreak on board the cruise ship. Norovirus is highly infectious. It can be transmitted by aerosol and the confined space on the ship coupled with the high density of staff and passengers provides the perfect environment for it to spread. Most patients suffer a short duration (24-48 hrs) of symptoms of vomiting and diarrhoea and do not require any support apart from oral rehydration salts. They may remain infectious for up to 48 hrs after the resolution of diarrhoea.

stem: A 40-year-old woman is referred to the Neurology Clinic due to a loss of sense of smell for the past nine months. She has also suffered from headaches, which have gradually become worse to a point where she is now suffering 6-8 headaches per week. Routine bloods are unremarkable. What is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: Olfactory groove meningiomas are slow-growing and fit with the picture seen here of many months of symptoms. Headaches are seen initially. These are followed by loss of the sense of smell, loss of taste and eventually blurred vision, memory loss, nausea, vomiting and personality changes. Magnetic resonance imaging to assess neuroanatomy and plan for potential resection is the next step.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic for review.On examination, he has developed thickened skin around his neck, his axillae and the palms of his hands, coupled with increased pigmentation. He has lost a few kilograms in weight over the past year, smokes five cigarettes per day and takes over-the- counter antacids for indigestion. His blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg and his pulse is 72 bpm and regular His body mass index is 23 kg/m. His abdomen is soft and non-tender and he is mildly tender in the epigastrium. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 105 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.5×10/L 4.0-11.0×10/L Platelets(PLT) 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 118 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glycated Hb(HbA1c) 43 mmol/mol 48 mmol/mol Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's skin changes?
explanation: This patient has skin thickening affecting the skin flexures, coupled with increased pigmentation. Taken together, this fits with a diagnosis of acanthosis nigricans. The condition is described in association with insulin resistance and is seen in obese patients with type ll diabetes, although in this case, the symptoms fit better with gastric adenocarcinoma, which is also associated with acanthosis nigricans. A number of solid malignancies may be associated with acanthosis nigricans, but stomach cancer that carries the strongest association.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis(RA). She works as a medical researcher and asks a number of questions about the prognosis of her condition. Which of the following is the biggest cause of increased mortality in patients with RA?
explanation: Across studies, there is nearly a 2-fold increase in standardised mortality rates for cardiovascular disease when patients with rheumatoid arthritis(RA) are compared to controls. Alongside infectious diseases, including pneumonia, the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events is significantly increased in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. This is,in fact, over and above what is expected when conventional cardiovascular risk markers are measured.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is referred to the Emergency Department by her General Practitioner (GP) for neutropenia. She has finished a cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer some two weeks earlier. Her GP has measured her full blood count on three occasions and found her neutrophil count to be0.3. She is apyrexial, with no signs of focal infection. Investigations: What is the most appropriate intervention? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 97 g/L 115-160 g/l White cell count(WCC) 4.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Neutrophils 0.1×10/L 1.5-8.0×10/L Platelets (PLT) 95×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 118μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
explanation: Neutropenia explanations Filgrastim is recombinant granulocyte-stimulating factor. It is indicated for primary prophylaxis of neutropenia and secondary prophylaxis of neutropenia associated with cytotoxic chemotherapy.In this case, the patient has persistent neutropenia and is at high risk of neutropenic sepsis. This drives the need for intervention with filgrastim. Treatment is continued daily until the neutrophil count is above 1.0 on two consecutive days.

stem: A 65-year-old man with heart failure presents to the Cardiology Ward with acute decompensation. He is treated with intravenous (IV) furosemide. Which of the following is the primary mode of action of furosemide?
options: Bicarbonate loss in the proximal tubule
explanation: Loop diuretics such as furosemide lead to a significant reduction in preload via diuresis in as little as 20-60 minutes. This is why IV furosemide is an effective part of the treatment armamentarium for acute left ventricular failure. Furosemide acts by inhibiting the Na+-K+-Cl- co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle which promotes sodium, water and potassium loss into the urine.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents to the Cardiology Clinic for review. She has hypertension and has had one previous admission with cardiac failure. Three months ago, she developed atrial fibrillation and had a failed electrical cardioversion two weeks ago. Her blood pressure is 145/84 mmHg and her pulse is 84 bpm in atrial fibrillation. There are no signs of cardiac failure on examination. Investigations: What is the most appropriate management of this patient's to reduce stroke risk? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/l 115-160 g/L White cell count(WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glycated Hb(HbA1c) 42 mmol/mol 48 mmol/mol
explanation: Atrial Fibrillation explanations Apixaban is a factor X inhibitor licensed for stroke prophylaxis in patients with atrial fibrillation. In this case, CHADS-VASc score components: female sex, age of 67 and the presence of both hypertension and congestive cardiac failure gives this patient a CHADS-VASc score of 4.This means she has an 8.5% per year risk of a stroke and anticoagulation is indicated. Factor X inhibitors have the advantage that they do not require monitoring with international normalised ratio (INR).

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner for review. She has primary amenorrhoea. She takes no medications and is otherwise well. Her blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 75 bpm and regular. She is 1.85m in height and has normal breast development and virtually no pubic or axillary hair. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient's height, female external genitalia and lack of pubic and axillary hair are highly suspicious of androgen insensitivity syndrome. Patients have an XYkaryotype but are androgen-resistant and have female external genitalia but usually have bilateral undescended testes. They may present soon after birth with bilateral inguinal hernias due to undescended testes. When sex hormones are measured, patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome actually have elevated testosterone.

stem: A58-year-old man who is known to have right lower lobe bronchiectasis presents to the Emergency Department holding a bowl containing 200 ml of blood which he has coughed up. He admits to coughing up small amounts of blood over the last three months and the frequency of haemoptysis has gradually increased. He was last admitted with right lower lobe pneumonia one year ago. His temperature is 36.7℃, pulse 105 bpm and regular and blood pressure 110/80 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 23 breaths/minute and he has decreased breath sounds at the right lung base. Pulse oximetry measures 90% on air. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 99 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count(WCC) 6.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 303×10/ 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 92 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Portable chest X-ray Patchy opacification-right base Which of the following is the most important intervention for the patient?
explanation: This patient has had large haemoptysis against a steady increase of episodes of haemoptysis over the past few months. A total of 200 ml of fresh blood is indicative of potentially life-threatening bleeding. It is likely that bronchiectasis with inflammation/erosion is compromising a pulmonary vessel. In this situation, where the patient is relatively stable, CT angiography can be performed,with the option to embolise a bleeding vessel with the help of interventional radiology. Bronchoscopy can also be considered in an emergency situation to achieve haemostasis.

stem: A 23-year-old man is reviewed in the Rheumatology Clinic after developing conjunctivitis, low back pain, oligoarthritis, dysuria and a psoriasis-like rash over both feet. He returned from a holiday to lbiza with friends some 2-3 weeks earlier. Which human leukocyte antigen(HLA) subtype is most associated with the patient's presentation?
explanation: This patient has features of reactive arthritis, including conjunctivitis, low back pain, oligoarthritis, dysuria and keratoderma blennorrhagica. The fact that he has just returned from a holiday raises the possibility that a sexually transmitted infection has acted as the trigger. HLA-B27 positivity is recognised as a risk factor for reactive arthritis. It is also well known to be associated with inflammatory bowel disease and the development of ankylosing spondylitis.

stem: A 43-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department complaining of persistent headaches which have increased in intensity over the past 2-3 weeks and that over the past day, she has been unable to open her right eye. She is usually well and takes no regular medication. Her right eye is nearly closed and, when it is opened, the pupil is deviated down and to the right. What is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: Posterior communicating artery aneurysms account for around 45% of intracerebral aneurysms and have a high rate of rupture. The findings on neurological examination are consistent with an oculomotor nerve palsy, with the eye looking down and out, and a ptosis. Oculomotor nerve palsies are seen most commonly with posterior communicating artery aneurysms because the artery runs close to the nerve. A magnetic resonance angiogram is the obvious next step in investigation.

stem: A73-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Department with worsening pain and stiffness affecting his left hip. He says this has developed over the past nine months and he is now unable to flex the hip properly and cannot walk more than a few metres without severe pain. He has hypertension but is otherwise well. His body mass index is 23 kg/m.Flexion of the left hip is severely limited by pain. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 243×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 118 mmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium 2.30 mmol/L 2.1-2.65 mmol/L Phosphate 1.1 mmol/L 0.8-1.5 mmol/L Alkaline phosphatase 389 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s hip pain?
explanation: Media explanations Paget's disease Unilateral joint destruction with limitation of movement and pain is the most common presentation of Paget's disease. Patients characteristically have normal calcium and phosphate levels and elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase, as seen here. A plain X-ray of the hip is the obvious next step; it is likely to show severe joint destruction with new bone formation. Bisphosphonates are the mainstay therapy for Paget's disease. They result in reduction in pain which is associated with a fall in alkaline phosphatase.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with epigastric pain and vomiting of sudden onset. He does not drink alcohol and does not suffer from gallstones. He has type ll diabetes, hypertension and generalised epilepsy. His temperature is 38.1°℃, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg and pulse 98 bpm and regular. He is exquisitely tender in the epigastrium. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 15.2×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 245×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 152μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Amylase 580 U/L 30-110 U/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's presentation?
explanation: Acute Pancreatitis explanations Sodium valproate is well recognised as a cause of acute pancreatitis, the likely diagnosis here, given the rise in amylase level and the acute presentation with epigastric pain and vomiting. Therapeutic agents are responsible for approximately 2% of cases of acute pancreatitis, and drugs definitely known to be associated with the disease include: · azathioprine · tetracyclines · sodium valproate ·methyldopa ·oestrogens ·furosemide ·6-mercaptopurine · corticosteroids · octreotide.

stem: A21-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department due to recurrent fevers over the past ten days. He has recently returned from working on his uncle's sheep farm in Northern Italy. He has felt unwell over the past few days with a fever of up to 38.5℃,a headache, back pain and a dry cough. His temperature is 38.5°℃, heart rate is 95 bpm and regular and blood pressure 100/70 mmHg. He complains of joint pains affecting his fingers, wrists, ankles and elbows. His chest is clear. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 135 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 6.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 102μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 89 mg/l 10 mg/l Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's pyrexia?
explanation: Brucellosis is a zoonosis, with sheep, cattle and pigs reported as possible vectors. In Europe, during the past few years, alpine regions have been associated with clusters of infection. The fact that this patient has been working on his uncle's farm implies close proximity to farm animals. Brucellosis is a rare disease, but still occurs in the low hundreds of cases per year in Europe. Fever, headache, dry cough and joint pains are all typical features. Brucellosis explanations The white cell count(WCC) is usually normal, although neutropenia can also be seen. Combination therapy with rifampicin and doxycycline for six weeks is the usual preferred intervention.Monotherapy is associated with high rates of relapse.

stem: An 85-year-old woman presents to the Outpatient Department complaining of pain across her lower back and right leg pain and weakness. Magnetic resonance imaging of the back arranged privately by her General Practitioner shows a right-sided synovial cyst leading to L3 nerve root compression. Which of the following symptoms would be expected most?
options: Abnormal sensation over the dorsum of the foot
Abnormal sensation over the front and inside of the lower thigh
explanation: The L3 nerve root is responsible for sensory supply to the anterior portion of the thigh down to the medial epicondyle of the femur. It fits with this patient's symptoms.Depending on her premorbid condition, she may be suitable for minimally invasive spinal surgery to correct the problem. Loss of motor function of L3 leads to weakness of knee extension.

stem: A 75-year-old man who has Parkinson's disease presents to the Acute Medical Ward with a urinary tract infection. He is hitting out at nursing staff with his stick, believing they are trying to poison him, taking out his intravenous lines and refusing to take medication orally. He is usually independent, with home help three times daily. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the patient's mental state?
explanation: Lorazepam is usually considered a second-line option in the treatment of delirium, the most likely cause of this patient's confusion. However, where there is underlying Parkinson's disease, haloperidol is not recommended because it can significantly worsen Parkinson's symptoms. The usual starting dose is 0.5mg IM. It can be delivered orally where patients are willing to take medication.

stem: A49-year-old man is diagnosed with a right deep vein thrombosis after presenting to the Emergency Department with a swollen right calf. He has end-stage renal disease, with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 12 ml/min. He is started on unfractionated heparin. What is the most appropriate choice for long-term anticoagulation?
explanation: This patient has chronic kidney disease stage 5, with a GFR15ml/min. Out of the options given, fondaparinux is injectable and, therefore,not desirable as a long-term intervention. The other options, apart from warfarin, are all subject to some degree of renal accumulation and are not recommended for patients with GFR15mlmin. A warfarin dose reduction of up to 30% vs that typically used in patients with normal renal function is usually required and an international normalised ratio3.0 should be avoided as it is associated with acute renal injury in patients with very low glomerular filtration rates.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an episode of jaundice related to underlying Gilbert syndrome. Which of the following is the immediate precursor to bilirubin?
explanation: Biliverdin is the direct precursor of bilirubin. It is formed by the breakdown of haem from senescent red blood cells. It is normally rapidly reduced by biliverdin reductase to bilirubin. Gilbert syndrome is caused by a defect in bilirubin uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase, which can lead to periodic elevations in bilirubin levels. Bilirubin is an antioxidant and patients with Gilbert syndrome are thought to have a lower rate of cardiac events as a consequence of elevated bilirubin levels.

stem: A38-year-old man presents to the Cardiology Clinic after suffering chest pain and palpitations during an amateur rugby match. He admits to episodes of chest pain while jogging over the past 2-3 months. He is a non-smoker who takes no regular medication. His blood pressure is 139/85 mmHg and his pulse is 66 bpm and regular. On examination of his chest, there is a forceful apex beat and a late systolic murmur which is augmented by the Valsalva manoeuvre. What is the most likely cause of the patient's cardiovascular symptoms?
explanation: The symptoms and examination findings indicate a diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Patients commonly experience angina, palpitations and syncopal episodes. The exertional nature of this patient’s symptoms suggest that he has marked septal hypertrophy with outflow tract obstruction. The left ventricular outflow tract obstruction is the likely cause of the late systolic murmur. The murmur can represent increased turbulence of blood as it passes through the left ventricular outflow tract, or it can sometimes be late systolic mitral regurgitation caused by systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. An echocardiogram is the initial investigation of choice and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may be useful to further describe the cardiac anatomy. Beta-blockers or disopyramide (a negative ionotropic drug) can suppress symptoms of left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, but they do not reduce the risk of ventricular arrhythmias. This patient should undergo risk stratification using the European Society of Cardiology's sudden cardiac death calculator to determine the need for an implantable cardioverter- defibrillator.

stem: 8 ):YY Jyi e1 A 20-year-old student nurse is reviewed in the Endocrine Clinic, having suffered a number of collapses while on attachment in the Emergency Department. Following one of these episodes, she had a finger-prick glucose measured at 2.7 mmol/L. Her blood pressure is 108/72 mmHg and her pulse is 73 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/l 115-160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 238×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 82 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Random glucose 5.2 mmol/L 7 mmol/L What is the most useful investigation for the patient's episodes of collapse?
options: Insulin, glucose and C-peptide at the same time as an attack
explanation: Hypoglycaemia Unrelated to Diabetes explanations Abuse of sulphonylureas and insulin is relatively rare among healthcare workers; however, it is recognised in healthcare workers, particularly in stressful work situations. The easiest way to confirm the diagnosis is by measuring glucose, C-peptide and insulin levels at the point of a collapse. Insulin abuse is associated with raised insulin and low C-peptide levels, together with hypoglycaemia. Sulphonylurea abuse is associated with raised insulin and C-peptide, and requires urinary analysis for sulphonylureas to confirm the diagnosis or to differentiate from an insulinoma. Where abuse of insulin or sulphonylureas is confirmed, cognitive behavioural therapy is the usual recommended intervention.

stem: A72-year-old man is assessed three weeks after a stroke. Part of the assessment involves measuring the Barthel index. Which of the following is assessed in the Barthel index?
options: Ability to draw a clock face
Ability to transfer from bed to chair
explanation: Ability to transfer from bed to chair is part of the activities of daily living measured in the Barthel index. Feeding, bathing, grooming, bowel control, bladder control, toilet use, mobility on a level surface and ability to climb stairs are other components of the score.

stem: A59-year-old man is referred to the Dermatology Clinic with worsening psoriasis. He usually has the typical rash affecting his elbows, knees and scalp, but he now has multiple psoriatic patches affecting his back and torso. He takes a number of medications for heart disease, diabetes and epilepsy, some of which have been changed recently, Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's worsening psoriasis?
explanation: Beta-blockers such as bisoprolol are well known to exacerbate symptoms of psoriasis. This may be related to increased T-cell and neutrophil activation as a result of increased intracellular phosphorylation. Switching the beta-blocker to an alternative antihypertensive medication should lead to an improvement in the psoriasis symptoms.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department, having been found unable to get up off the floor outside the local supermarket. She is known to be an intravenous drug user. Her temperature is 37.9°℃, blood pressure is 122/85 mmHg and her heart rate is 89 bpm and regular. There is a large injecting abscess in her left groin. She displays facial grimacing and neck stiffness and finds it difficult to open her mouth. Her abdomen is also rigid and she appears to have involuntary muscle spasms. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 104 g/L 115-160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 13.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 123×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 135 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 105μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 123 mg/l 10 mg/l What is the most appropriate next step in treatment for this patient?
explanation: Tetanus explanations This patient has tetanus as a result of the introduction of Clostridium tetani, most likely via the injecting abscess in her groin. Her neurological symptoms are related to the tetanus toxin,neutralisation of which with human tetanus immunoglobulin is the most appropriate next step. Without tetanus immunoglobulin being administered first, antibiotics are ineffective and debridement may actually worsen symptoms because it liberates more of the toxin.

stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance. He is incontinent of urine and bed-bound. He has been sent in as the district nurse is very concerned about a sacral pressure sore. Examination reveals a large sacral sore, with visible bone at its base. There is adherent slough, bleeding and pus. What grade is the patient's pressure sore?
explanation: In a grade 4 ulcer, there is full-thickness tissue loss leading to exposed bone or tendon. There may be undermining and tunnelling where a superficial tissue layer is exposed, but there is extensive loss underneath the area. They can extend into adjacent structures, eg into muscle or a joint capsule. Debridement of a grade 4 ulcer is essential, as is management using a pressure-relieving mattress and appropriate intravenous antibiotics.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has rheumatoid arthritis, which is managed with methotrexate. Over the past few months, she has developed problems with a dry mouth, dry and gritty eyes and intermittent parotid gland swelling. Physical examination identifies swelling over the parotids. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/L 115-160 g/L White cell count (WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 172×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 82 μmol/L 50-120μmol/L Autoantibodies Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and rheumatoid factor positive Which other autoantibody is most likely to be associated with this patient's eye condition?
explanation: This patient has symptoms consistent with drying of the mucus membranes, dry eyes and parotitis. Taken together with ANA positivity, the possibility of Sjgren syndrome is raised. Sjgren syndrome is also associated with positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, which have particular significance in pregnant women because they may lead to neonatal heart block. Apart from immune-modulating agents, symptoms respond well to artificial tears and artificial saliva supplementation.

stem: A 45-year-old man of West-African origin is reviewed in the Renal Clinic. Despite treatment with ramipril eplerenone and dapagliflozin, he has persistent proteinuria and his glomerular filtration rate(GFR) is deteriorating. His blood pressure is 151/89 mmHg and his pulse is 71 bpm and regular. There is pitting oedema of both ankles. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin(Hb) 115 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.6×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 249×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 172 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine 1.8g in 24 hours Renal biopsy Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis What mutation is most likely to be associated with the patient's presentation?
explanation: APOL1 gene mutations are protective against sleeping sickness and are more common in the West African AAGPAT2 population. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is also more common in the West African population and progresses more rapidly despite intervention in patients carrying the APOL1 mutation. The gene is a target for silencing ribonucleic acid(RNA) therapies which is a current research focus. The AGPAT2 gene carries the genetic code for AGPAT2 which drives triglyceride and phospholipid synthesis. Mutations in the gene cause congenital generalised lipodystrophy.

stem: A 64-year-old man has peptic ulcer disease and is poorly compliant with proton pump inhibitors.He has been recommended to undergo partial gastrectomy because of pyloric stenosis due to recurrent ulceration, but he has refused. He is admitted with vomiting over the past 24 hours. He is unable to keep anything down. What is the expected picture on blood gas analysis?
explanation: This patient is vomiting hydrochloric acid. This leads to loss of both hydrogen ions and chloride ions, leading to the development of hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Loss of potassium ions also occurs, leading to hypokalaemia. Chloride-containing fluid replacement is the most important intervention in correcting hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He has always struggled with sports and exercise and he is now finding it dificult to climb the stairs. He gets muscle cramps after only short bursts of exercise. He has an elder brother who is 23 years old and similarly affected. His sister has no health issues. Examination reveals wasting of the proximal muscles of the lower limbs, with bilateral calf hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type l
explanation: This patient's pattern of proximal limb weakness with distal hypertrophy, where the weakness has gradually increased over a number of years,fits well with a diagnosis of BMD. The pattern of inheritance, where only men have symptoms, is consistent with an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern. Symptoms are similar to those of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, but much less severe.CK is increased in patients with BMD and may be up to 50 times the upper limit of normal. Cardiomyopathy and atrial arrhythmias are common long-term sequelae of the condition.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with nausea and vomiting. Her only medication is indapamide for the treatment of hypertension. Her blood pressure is 142/95 mmHg, with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Investigations: There is concern that indapamide may have contributed to pre-renal failure. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 129 g/l 115-160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 11.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 238×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Which of the following best represents the diuretic site of action of indapamide?
explanation: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It acts in the distal tubule to reduce distal luminal reabsorption of Na.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an erythematous crusting lesion on the left-hand side of his chin. There are smaller areas of erythema, consistent with infection, on his chin, which he says may have been due to him scratching. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Topical therapies are the intervention of choice for impetigo, the likely diagnosis here. The crusted lesion with smaller 'satellite'areas of erythema spread by touch is typical of the condition. A Cochrane meta- analysis suggests both mupirocin and Fucidin are potential treatment options. Non-bullous impetigo is most commonly caused either by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus.

stem: A 74-year-old man with metastatic squamous cell lung cancer is admitted to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting and dehydration. He has undergone palliative radiotherapy one month earlier. His blood pressure is 120/82 mmHg and his pulse is 89 bpm and regular. He is drowsy and mildly confused. He has a body mass index of 21 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 111 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 12.1×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets (PLT) 152×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 3.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 141μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium 2.95 mmol/L 2.1-2.65 mmol/l Phosphate 0.6 mmol/L 0.8-1.5 mmol/L What is the most likely cause of the patient's hypercalcaemia?
explanation: Calcium homeostasis,vitamin Dand hypercalcaemia explanations Parathyroid hormone-related peptide(PTHrP) production accounts for as much as 80% of cases of hypercalcaemia of malignancy. It is seen in squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus and in patients with renal, bladder, breast or ovarian carcinoma.The low phosphate level here is a strong pointer to PTHrP as the cause of this patient's symptoms. Rehydration with normal saline can lead to an immediate reduction in serum calcium levels, which can be further reduced by using bisphosphonates. Treatment to reduce tumour burden can help further control hypercalcaemia.

stem: A 19-year-old man is referred to the Renal Clinic with haematuria, hypertension and a mildly elevated creatinine level. His father has haematuria, renal impairment and deafness, and his sister has haematuria but is not affected by renal impairment and has normal hearing. His blood pressure is 152/90 mmHg,and his pulse is 72 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no masses. His body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m2. Which defect is most likely to underlie the patient's chronic kidney disease?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged Alport syndrome is the most likely diagnosis here, with an X-Linked dominant inheritance pattern given men in the family are more affected than women. The condition is caused by a defect in type IV collagen synthesis, leading to basement membrane dysfunction and progressive glomerular disease. It is characterised by haematuria, sensorineural deafness, hypertension and progressive renal impairment. Proteinuria develops with hypertension, and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition is indicated to slow the progression of renal disease. End-stage kidney disease develops in men on average between the ages of 16 and 37.

stem: A19-year-old student presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review.She has suffered from increasingly severe back pain and stiffness, which starts in the early hours of the morning and often lasts until lunchtime before easing. She has not gained any relief from taking regular ibuprofen. Examination reveals pain over the sacroiliac joints and limited forward and lateral flexion of the lumbar spine. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/l 115-160 g/l White cell count(WCC) 8.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 291×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 81 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte sedimentation 57 mm/hr 10 mm/hr rate(ESR) C-reactive protein (CRP) 65 mg/l 10 mg/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Ankylosing Spondyitis Media explanations This patient has evidence of inflammation of the sacroiliac joints and limited movement affecting the lumbar spine. Given it is worse in the morning, takes a number of hours to resolve and is associated with raised inflammatory markers, ankylosing spondylitis is the most likely diagnosis. The condition may also be associated with plantar fasciitis and inflammatory bowel disease.Physiotherapy is crucial in the management of the condition to maintain flexibility. If pain and symptoms are not controlled following a second alternative non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, progression to an anti-tumour necrosis factor agent is potentially indicated.

stem: A72-year-old retired plumber presents to the Respiratory Clinic for review. He has suffered from a chronic dry cough and shortness of breath for the past year. His symptoms have not improved despite a corticosteroid and salbutamol inhaler. He smokes ten cigarettes per day. His blood pressure is 147/90 mmHg, his pulse is 88 bpm and regular. There are coarse crackles throughout both lung fields on auscultation of the chest. His body mass index(BMI) is 26 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 159 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 10.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 252×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(NA+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/l 50-120 μmol/L Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV)/forced vital capacity(FVC) FVC 65% of predicted What is the most likely cause for the patient's shortness of breath?
explanation: This patient is a retired plumber, which raises the possibility of exposure to asbestos and consequent asbestos-related pulmonary fibrosis.The marked reduction in FVC, coupled with a normal FEV/FVC ratio, is consistent with this as the underlying diagnosis. Even with the smoking history reported here, the lung function picture makes pulmonaryfibrosis much more likely than COPD as the cause of his symptoms.A chest X-ray and high-resolution computed tomography (CT) scan are the appropriate next steps.

stem: A38-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with excessive sweating, acne, hypertension and a change in her facial features over the past year. Her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg and pulse is 72 bpm and regular. She has a prominent mandible and macroglossia. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. Which initial blood test is most useful in making the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: This patient's symptoms, including acne, sweating, a prominent lower jaw, macroglossia and hypertension, all fit with possible acromegaly. IGF-1 is an ideal initial screening test because it has a half-life of 15 hours and values closely correlate with growth hormone levels. Approximately 30 nmol/L is the upper limit of the normal range in a woman of this age. An oral glucose tolerance test, with growth hormone measurement, is used to confirm the diagnosis, coupled with pituitary magnetic resonance imaging(MRI). Trans-sphenoidal excision of an underlying pituitary adenoma is indicated. Patients may be pretreated with a growth hormone antagonist to improve metabolic status before surgery.

stem: An 18-year-old man comes to the Outpatient Department for review. He has diarrhoea related to pancreatic insufficiency and his pancreatic enzyme supplementation is increased. He asks about vitamin supplementation. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for vitamin supplementation?
explanation: This patient has cystic fibrosis and pancreatic insufficiency. Despite pancreatic enzyme supplementation, patients with pancreatic insufficiency still suffer from deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins. For this reason, supplementation with the range of fat-soluble vitamins A,D,E and K is recommended.

stem: A34-year-old man with known epilepsy is admitted to the Emergency Department following a prolonged tonic-clonic seizure at the local supermarket. He is thought to be poorly compliant with antiepileptic medication and is a heavy user of alcohol. His blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg and his pulse is 82 bpm and regular. On arrival at the Emergency Department, he suffers a prolonged seizure which fails to terminate. Glucose by fingerprick testing is 7.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation: Intravenous(IV) lorazepam is the intervention of choice for status epilepticus. Graduated doses of lorazepam in 1mg IV increments are given to control seizures. Airway support is likely to be required as sedation is increased. In the event that IV access has not been obtained, then buccal midazolam can be given as a temporary measure.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who works at the animal house at the local medical research facility presents to the Respiratory Clinic. She has a cough, shortness of breath and wheeze which increases through the working week and only improves at weekends and during periods of holiday. She has just returned from a holiday abroad and a physical exam is entirely normal. Her peak flow is 520 litres/minute (545 predicted). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Provision of a respirator for work
explanation: This patient has symptoms of uncontrolled asthma which worsen during the working week and improve during periods of time away from work. This is most consistent with a diagnosis of occupational asthma.

stem: A45-year-old man is reviewed before discharge following a paracetamol overdose. He took 30 tablets after his wife left him. He has also recently become unemployed. He had been difficulty sleeping, with low appetite and mood, and had contemplated stockpiling paracetamol tablets for a while. He tells you that he is not suicidal now. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: 28 days of amitriptyline 100 mg once daily (OD) and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
Seven days of citalopram 20 mg OD and CBT
Seven days of diazepam 5mg twice daily(BD) and CBT
28 days of duloxetine 60 mg OD and CBT
CBT but no plans for medication
explanation: In this situation with a self-harm event and contemplation of further overdoses, it is prudent to minimise access to potentially harmful agents. Although selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors(SSRIs) are relatively safe in overdose, it is prudent to limit the patient to seven days of medication. SSRls are, of course, safer in overdose versus tricyclic antidepressants. The prescription should be combined with cognitive behavioural therapy, and on successful review in the clinic the prescription for citalopram can be extended. Longer duration follow up after SSRI prescription is not advised because of the risk of activation and actual increased risk of suicidal behaviour.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of muscle pains which have increased over the past few days. He has recently been diagnosed with ischaemic heart disease and has started a number of new medications,including ramipril, simvastatin, aspirin and amlodipine. He has recently also switched to a plant-based diet. His blood pressure is 115/74 mmHg and his pulse is 74 bpm and regular. His heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 135 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 242×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 118μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Creatine kinase(CK) 1357 U/L 22-198 U/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's elevated CK?
explanation: Liver Enzyme Inhibition Media explanations Grapefruit juice is a potent inhibitor of CYP3A4,the cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for the metabolism of simvastatin. Consumption of grapefruit juice drives the accumulation of simvastatin and this, in turn, leads to myopathy, which is responsible for this patient's muscle pains and the significant elevation in creatine kinase. Grapefruit juice should be discontinued. Switching to atorvastatin over the longer term will significantly reduce the risk of myopathy, even when grapefruit juice is consumed.

stem: A 38-year-old man who has ulcerative colitis comes to the Outpatient Department for review. He complains of vague right upper quadrant pains, night sweats and being off his food for the past few months. He also has itching and tiredness. His ulcerative colitis is well controlled. There is one finger-breadth hepatomegaly on abdominal palpation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 127 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 112×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 145 IU/L 7-50 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 438 IU/L 44-147 IU/L Bilirubin 25μmol/L 5.1-17 μmol/L Which of the following is the most useful next investigation to elucidate the underlying cause?
explanation: This patient has progressive symptoms of liver dysfunction, coupled with an obstructive picture on liver function testing, against a background of ulcerative colitis. This fits with a diagnosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis, which is more common in men and occurs in 5% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Up to 70% of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis are thought to have inflammatory bowel disease, of whom 80% have ulcerative colitis. MRCP is the investigation of choice to demonstrate areas of biliary tract dilatation and stricturing, which are characteristic of the disease. The only successful intervention for advanced primary sclerosing cholangitis is liver transplantation.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has been treated for epilepsy for the past three months following a second tonic- clonic seizure. She is stable and well, but her partner tells you she refuses to go out because she is scared of it being unsafe, with no ability to get help or to escape from a situation. Physical examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely psychiatric diagnosis?
explanation: Agoraphobia fits with this patient's symptoms. It is characterised by anxiety in situations where the person feels their environment to be unsafe without any easy way to escape. People can report symptoms of agoraphobia in a range of situations such as on public transport, in an open space, in a shopping centre or simply being outside the home. In this case, the symptoms have been precipitated by the onset of epilepsy. Cognitive behavioural therapy to help the patient adjust to the 'new normal' following her diagnosis of epilepsy is the most appropriate intervention.

stem: A 62-year-old man is referred to the Renal Clinic. He has recently been started on ramipril 10 mg for presumed diabetic nephropathy, but this has been discontinued due to a rise in potassium. His blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, and his pulse is 72 bpm and regular.His chest is clear, there is no ankle swelling. His body mass index(BMI) is 31 kg/m. Investigations: What is the most likely cause of the rise in K+ seen on starting ramipril? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 130 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count 8.0×10/L 4-11×10/L (WCC) Platelets(PLT) 249×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L 4.7 mmol/L Potassium(K+) Increase to 5.9 mmol/l one week after starting angiotensin- 3.5-5.0 mmol/L converting enzyme inhibitor(ACEi), repeated at the hospital 131μmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 50-120 μmol/L Stable at 132 mmol/l one week after starting ACEi Glycated Hb 48 mmol/mol (HbA1c) Urine Protein 1+, blood negative
explanation: Renal tubular acidosis type 4 is associated with resistance to aldosterone because of intrinsic renal damage. This is often unmasked when patients take a drug which is recognised to increase K+ such as an ACEi or an angiotensin receptor blocker. The lack of rise in Cr associated with ACEi initiation points to this as the diagnosis, rather than renovascular disease.

stem: A59-year-old man with advanced colorectal cancer is admitted to the Emergency Department with febrile neutropenia. His current treatment regimen includes the use of irinotecan. What is the mode of action of irinotecan?
explanation: Irinotecan is a derivative of camptothecin and a specific inhibitor of DNA topoisomerase l. It is metabolised by carboxylesterases to SN-38, which was found to be more active than irinotecan in purified topoisomerasel and more cytotoxic than irinotecan against several murine and human tumour cell lines. Inhibition of DNA topoisomerase Iby irinotecan or SN-38 induces single-strand DNA lesions which block the DNA replication fork and drive the cytotoxicity associated with irinotecan use.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with dysphagia and vomiting of solid food, retrosternal pain and weight loss which has gradually worsened over the past three months. He has lost 12 kg in weight. He continues to smoke 20 cigarettes per day. His blood pressure is 132/85 mmHg and his pulse is 88 bpm and regular. There is mild epigastric tenderness on abdominal palpation, with a palpable liver edge. His body mass index is 21 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 91 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 167×10/ 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: Oesophageal tumours Media explanations This patient has progressive dysphagia and weight loss, with a blood picture showing anaemia. In an elderly smoker, there is high suspicion of underlying oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Endoscopy with a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis is the next appropriate step.The fact that a liver edge is palpable raises the possibility of liver metastases.In a high percentage of cases of oesophageal cancer, there are metastases already at the point of diagnosis, precluding oesophagectomy and making stenting the most appropriate intervention.

stem: A 43-year-old man with chronic alcoholism is referred to the Falls Clinic. The main finding is an ataxic gait. Which of the following is most likely to have been damaged by chronic alcohol abuse?
options: Dorsal nucleus of the vagus nerve
Triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus
explanation: Chronic alcohol abuse leads to atrophy of the cerebellar vermis, which accounts for the ataxic gait seen here. The prevalence of vermian atrophy is estimated to be up to 27% from autopsy specimens. It is thought to occur from both direct alcohol-related neurotoxicity and thiamine deficiency. Early changes affect the anterior superior vermis, where volume loss occurs. Progression can involve the posterior inferior vermis and the anterior lobes of the cerebellum, which is part of the triad of symptoms seen in Wernicke's encephalopathy.

stem: A 22-year-old man of African-American origin presents to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath and extreme lethargy. He is planning a trip to Vietnam and has begun malaria prophylaxis. His pulse is 95 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg. He has jaundiced sclerae. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 87 g/L 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 6.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 241×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the patient most likely to have received?
explanation: This patient is of African heritage and has been taking malaria prophylaxis. It appears he has become significantly anaemic, raising the possibility of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase(G6PD) deficiency and an acute haemolytic crisis because of the medication. Out of the options given, primaquine is the most likely cause of the haemolysis. It acts as an oxidising agent.

stem: A35-year-old man who is known to have long-standing HIV infection is brought to the Emergency Department following a grand mal seizure. He is drowsy and confused with a GCS of 13. His temperature is 38.0℃, blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg, pulse is 94 bpm and regular. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 115 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 4.9×10/L 4-11×10/L CD4 count Platelets(PLT) 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 129 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 102 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L CRP 87 mg/L 10 mg/l Leptomeningeal and pachymeningeal MRI brain enhancement. Dilated perivascular spaces What is the most likely cause of his neurological presentation?
explanation: This patient has evidence of acute infection with a very low CD4 count and signs of meningism with raised intracranial pressure. The MRI brain picture is consistent with cryptococcal infection where there is dilatation and sometimes cyst formation within the perivascular spaces. An elevated opening pressure is seen on lumbar puncture, usually with lymphocytes present in the cerebrospinal fluid. Glucose is depressed and protein levels are elevated. Amphotericin B is a potential initial intervention.

stem: A 19-year-old man with hereditary spherocytosis is reviewed in the Surgical Clinic before elective splenectomy. He asks about risks of infection. Which of the following is the patient at greatest risk of infection from?
explanation: Serious infections with s. pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria meningitidis are significantly increased in patients who have undergone splenectomy because resistance to capsulated bacteria is reduced. The risk of overwhelming infection is put at around 4% and is highest in the first two years after splenectomy. Long-term oral penicillin prophylaxis is indicated.
